source.title: Disparity Between Batches as a Signal for Early Stopping

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies the fraction of randomly assigned training labels and reports training and test curves, using those experiments to study label noise and generalization.
record.gate_note: The paper reports label-noise experiments, including curves in Figs. 5, 17, 21 and 24. It does not state numerical training-error results or explicitly describe whether fully random labels reach zero training error. Results cited from other studies are not included.
record.test_reason: The study trains standard networks with SGD on randomly relabeled image datasets and reports training and test errors across noise levels. These experiments bear on V1 and V4, although several relevant curves cannot be read from the supplied text.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes two secondary observations: gradient disparity reflects label-noise levels early in training, and the authors interpret low MNIST test error at 75% noise as resistance to memorization. Their main conclusion is that gradient disparity provides an effective early-stopping signal, particularly with limited or noisy data. The MNIST interpretation does not itself establish failure to fit corrupted training labels.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains image-classification networks on datasets with randomly assigned labels at varying fractions, rather than focusing on fitting a completely random labeling as the primary outcome. It reports training curves but does not state whether full random labeling reaches zero training error.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and label-noise fraction; the text notes that the MNIST result at 75% label noise differs from a simple expectation of memorization.

fits_no_version.finding: Gradient disparity distinguishes label-noise levels early in training and often tracks test error better than the generalization gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient disparity can indicate label corruption and signal when to stop training.

record.problems: The relevant training-error results are presented in figures without stated numerical values or a textual conclusion about zero training error under fully random labels. The explicitly described MNIST test-error observation is qualitative.
record.rows_left_out: No other rows were kept. Other label-noise curves in Figs. 17, 21 and 24 are figure-only and do not add a separately stated result about the versions beyond the extracted full-random-label training-error curve and the textual 75% MNIST observation.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training error and chance test error at 100% random labels cannot be established from the supplied figure text.
Training-time ratios and convergence slowdown with increasing label corruption.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit at every noise fraction cannot be established from the supplied curves.
Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting and whether removing regularization preserves true-label generalization.
Direct comparison of learning shared real-label patterns with memorizing corrupted examples over training. The paper cites this ordering as motivation but does not separately measure the two groups.

missing.what: The explicit reversal of the noise–test-error relationship: the clean-label ResNet-18 has 99% test error, while higher-noise networks have lower test error and loss. rows_left_out mentions Fig. 24 but incorrectly treats its findings as figure-only and adding no distinct result.

Without early stopping, training continues until cross-entropy loss is below 0.01, including 50%-random-label conditions. Final test errors for 0% versus 50% random labels are 4.96% versus 25.72% for MNIST/AlexNet and 64.19% versus 75.96% for CIFAR-10/ResNet-18. These document near-perfect noisy-label fitting with remaining test signal, but do not establish the complete noise sweep.
missing.locator: Table 12(a–d), No ES column; Appendix I

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source of these versions. Figure captions identify relevant experiments but provide no readable curve values. Neither unreadable curves nor low test error alone justify a negative verdict on random-label fitting.

versions.untested_parts: The figure shows training error across label-noise levels, including 100%, but the text does not state whether training error reaches zero or near zero, or give test error at chance.
The paper does not report training-time ratios or explicitly state how convergence time changes with the fraction of corrupted labels.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs are not tested.
The paper reports test-error behavior across label-noise levels, but does not state that training error remains perfect at every level or that test error rises steadily toward chance.
The paper does not test whether regularization prevents fitting random labels or whether removing it harms generalization on true labels.
The paper does not test the ordering or difference between learning real-label patterns and memorizing noise over training.
